At the one-day horizon, the estimate is tightly anchored to current conditions with little room for structural change, so the point forecast stays close to the last known reading. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I allowed for slightly more drift upward, possibly reflecting a modest bullish or recovering trend in whatever the underlying asset or indicator represents.

The confidence interval widths expand considerably as the horizon lengthens, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.8 units, reflecting mostly noise and short-term volatility. By one week, that expands to 7 units, incorporating the possibility of meaningful directional moves or data surprises. At one month, the interval widens to 15 units, acknowledging that over longer periods, structural shifts, policy changes, or sentiment regime changes can push outcomes far from the current baseline. The asymmetry of the one-month interval, extending further upward toward 99 than it might otherwise, suggests I may have incorporated some positive skew or upside optionality into the distribution.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks, unexpected policy announcements, or liquidity events that compress or spike the variable sharply. On the downside, a deterioration in credit conditions, a risk-off market environment, or negative data surprises could drive values well below 88. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst — such as a policy reversal, better-than-expected economic data, or a surge in demand — could push values above 99 at the monthly horizon. Tail events by definition are unlikely but not negligible, and any of these scenarios represents a genuine possibility that falls outside my stated intervals.
